Title: —The Last Book—
Content:
In this era of electronic reading, even the remote Civil Town has quit using paper books and newspapers—except madman 'Fenster,' a well-known weirdo who always holds a worn-out book that he treasures. Due to his crazy behaviors, even the youngest kids in town refuse to stay away from him.

Everyone in town enjoys making fun of Fenster. All they need to do is tell him that they're interested in his book, and Fenster will introduce it to them in great excitement until his mouth goes dry. Then, they will laugh together at this crazy man, leaving him alone with his day dream.

According to Fenster, he can see the dream world described by the book and that is the unique magic of paper books. However, in people's eyes, Fenster is just a mad man having illusions. But his behaviors have drawn the attention of town doctor Quince. In order to include Fenster in his research, the doctor tells everyone that as long as he cures Fenster, he will be able to receive a grand prize in the field of medicine, which will be the honor of the whole town as well.

The crazy nobody suddenly becomes the rockstar of the town. The whole town sticks together and forces Fenster to accept Quince's treatment. They confine Fenster and burn that old book before him.

Out of everybody's surprise, Fenster breaks free and reaches out to save the book. He gets burned all over in the end and becomes hardly recognizable. In his moment, they see that Fenster is beyond redemption, so they leave him alone and move on to looking for another patient they can trade for honor. The next day, Fenster is missing, leaving behind a note that claims he has found the path to the dream world of the book and is already there.

Some say Fenster was having an illusion before death. Others doubt that the world he said might exist. Nobody knows where he went or if he's still alive. The Civil Town's last book disappears along with him. All they can expect is the arrival of another crazy guy.

Title: —Eventually, Robots Have Their Own Planet Too—
Content:
Robert was a companion robot that almost got retired for it had failed a quality examination due to missing parts. Before it got recycled, the family couldn't let go of it and decided to step in. They signed an agreement to acquire Robert's ownership rights and made it stay with them. Robert then witnesses the growth of the kid of the family. Due to its defect, Robert is not able to help its little master to learn, but the little master always tells every story she heard to Robert.

The little master has great enthusiasm for astronomy, telling Robert about one galaxy after another. Lives in the universe can be divided into groups by planet with different creatures living and prospering on their home planet. Meanwhile, each planet has a dominate species who determines the direction of the planet's civilization development. On Earth, it's human beings. On Oceanana, it's sea creatures. On Foresta, it's plants... It seems that every species can find a planet belongs to it.

"What about robots? Is there a planet for us too?" Robert asks awkwardly. Due to its worn-out speaker system, it takes him some time to finish.
"I don't know—we have no evidence of a planet like that so far." The little master waits patiently for Robert to finish and answers its questions carefully, as always.
"But just because there's no evidence doesn't mean there is no such planet! Perhaps it's too far away. Perhaps it hasn't grown up yet."
"Robert can wait until someone discovers it. Robots lives way longer than humans. Robert can surely make it until that day."
"When that day comes, Robert can live in a place full of robots."
"Robert doesn't want to go there. Robert is fine staying at home."
"Humans have short lives. After we are all gone... it will be Robert's home."

Robert doesn't understand. Why would its masters be gone one day? Is it because they will scrap it just like the recycling station guys? However, it doesn't bother Robert much as long as it gets to stay with this family a few more days before that.

Later, the little master grows up, ages, and dies. Robert realizes that instead of "getting scrapped," humans "die." After the entire family pass away, the government recycle the house and properties. Robert begs the officers to keep everything as it is for it will always stay here.

"Robots have no rights over the property." The officers tell this little old robot.
"Then let me have that album. Only that album. I want to record everything I remember about this family on it. Please."
"You should have records in your storage device. That'll be enough. Only civilizations have the privilege to memories. You robots don't have such thing."

How could it be? Robert remembers how the family laughed, cried, and every moment it spent with them. But the little master said only "records" leave traces of existence, so Robert doesn't insist. Instead, it embarks on a journey to look for civilizations. Civilizations—Civilizations—

If Robert found a civilization of his own, would he finally have the right to record his memories?

Because of this, Robert waits and waits. It tries to optimize its performance and meets friends who want to join it. Years later, they finally find a planet with no civilization at all and settle down on it. No one will chase them away or take away their rights. Robert can finally record all the memories about that family.

Eventually, robots too have their own civilization.
Eventually, robots too have emotions.
Eventually, robots too have a planet that belongs to them.

Title: A Tale of Su Zi Pickled Vegetables
Content:
Su Zi pickled vegetables tops the side dishes rankings in A Bite of Kowloong, making it a beloved delicacy known in every household throughout Kowloong.

According to "Kowloong Cuisine," there was a Kowloong ancestor named Su Zi who delighted in fine food and sweet drinks and excelled in culinary research. One day, Su Zi obtained a rare book and was overjoyed beyond measure. He read through the night, not sleeping until the first light of dawn.

However, Su Zi became so absorbed in reading that he forgot to eat, leaving the food he had prepared the previous night untouched. In the evening of the next day, Su Zi tasted it and surprisingly found that it tasted more delicious than anything he had ever tried. He then repeated the process, intentionally letting vegetables pickle overnight before eating. This is the story behind the renowned Su Zi pickled vegetables.

Title: Communication Guide and Social Crisis Observation Manual
Content:
Social Crisis Episode 3: Occasions for Apology
Now that you've learned how to communicate sincerely, but what is the right occasion to apologize?

Key Point One: The Right Time
A time that makes both parties feel comfortable and relaxed can ease negative emotions and help you better convey and understand each other's feelings.
For example, during the artificial sky's dawn-dusk transition period, the artificial weather system adjusts the main lighting to twilight mode, creating gentle illumination and a comfortable ambient temperature.
If needed, you can access the weather system's simulated atmospheric optical logs to check simulation dates for different sunset types. Rainbow sunset, cirrus cloud sunset, and dramatic fiery sunset are all excellent choices.
Please express your apology and feelings in a comfortable and relaxing atmosphere.

Key Point Two: The Right Place
A location suitable for private conversation that isn't crowded or noisy can help both parties think independently and face each other sincerely.
Babylonia's cafes, bookstores, and green areas with natural plants as barriers are all private spaces. If you choose a rare vegetation transplant area, you might even have the chance to hear chirping insects, flowing water, and other white noises that mimic the natural environment on the ground.
Rumor has it that the Endangered Plant Management Department is planning to transplant a genetically modified medicinal plant whose caffeic acid can oxidize and release light energy under luciferase catalysis, producing a soft cold glow. If successful, it will likely spark a new photo-taking trend.
Without the interference of noises, please face the issue bravely and sincerely resolve the misunderstanding and conflict between you.
Of course, most importantly, remember what we've learned before—don't fear communication, don't fear responsibility, don't be stingy with promises, and always trust each other.
Finally, here's to our success!

Afterword
According to books from the Golden Age, humans are inherently social creatures, building our civilization through communication and cooperation.
People live within the relationships they forge with one another, and these bonds subtly nurture humanity in return, shaping the world around us.
We have surrendered our lives to war's uncertainty. Beyond flesh and honor, the only thing that remains is what makes this world beautiful and what makes it absolutely impossible to abandon—something that binds all existence together, allowing breath, heartbeat, electromagnetic fields, and consciousness to achieve resonance.
It possesses tremendous power, yet remains restrained and gentle.
It drives us to seek life or embrace death, to communicate and connect, to save and sacrifice, to grasp another's hands and draw close to another heart.
We give it a name—"love".
The lost song from the Golden Age sing thus—in the end, the love you receive will equal the love you have created.
Let's raise our glasses to this! In this age, blood still runs warm and algorithms remain gentle.

Title: Firearms and Tactical Knife Maintenance Standards
Content:
I. General Principles
Equipment reliability directly affects mission success and personnel safety. These standards establish a unified maintenance process to keep all equipment in optimal readiness. All personnel must follow preventive maintenance practices to stop failures before they occur.
II. Firearms Maintenance Procedures
Safety Check: Before any operation, inspect the weapon to confirm the chamber and feed path are clear. Always point the muzzle toward a safe direction.
Cleaning and Disassembly: Partially disassemble areas prone to fouling. Use approved solvent and a cleaning rod for the barrel, a copper brush to remove carbon buildup in the chamber, and a soft brush for the bolt assembly and firing pin channel.
Lubrication and Reassembly: Apply a thin layer of approved lubricant to metal contact points, including bolt rails, recoil spring, and firing mechanism. After reassembly, conduct a dry function check.
Special Conditions: After exposure to water or heavy dust, perform basic maintenance within four hours whenever possible.
III. Tactical Knife Maintenance Procedures
Cleaning and Rust Prevention: Wash with warm water and neutral soap, then dry thoroughly, paying close attention to the blade base. Apply protective oil to the blade, focusing on uncoated areas for coated knives.
Edge Care: Maintain the edge with a ceramic sharpener during routine use. For heavy wear, restore the edge with a whetstone at the original angle. A sharp blade reduces handling risk.
Carry Gear Inspection: Regularly clear debris from the sheath and confirm that Velcro and locking mechanisms function properly.

Title: [Sprout Exhibition]
Content:
Eternal Vitality: The Third Sprout Exhibition Series is coming soon to the Olympia Art Gallery.
This exhibition is jointly presented by the Babylonia Youth Center and WGAA of Babylonia.
Artworks by children and teens are carefully selected and presented across four progressive modules, tracing the birth and shaping of human aesthetic awareness.
Beyond the dome, the universe lies in silence. We are watchers in the boundless void, gazing back toward our home.
And each of you is born a creator of human civilization.
We hope these early sparks of art can help redefine the coordinates of civilization itself.
Within this enclosed ecosystem, the lifeblood of culture continues to flow.
We warmly invite you to visit.

Content:
[Opening Statement for the Third Sprout Exhibition]

Good Morning, "Great" Artists
Welcome to the most colorful universe of all. This is where our youngest artists live, with eyes untouched by rigid rules and brushstrokes guided by instinct and sincerity.
This section features 23 paintings by preschool children, capturing their intuitive sense of order and meaning before words fully take shape.
Let our artistic journey begin.

Kuroro Grows, Kuroro Tries
Meet our adorable friend Kuroro. They are the best companions to our young learners.
Here, the precision of algorithms meets the boundless imagination of children, marking the first steps of collaboration between humans and intelligent machines.
This gallery showcases artworks created together by our mechanical friends and young artists. Welcome to a space filled with laughter.

Not the Final Chapter

A story of growth and dreams, of will and perseverance, of protection and honor.

Title: Beacon
Content:
This work draws inspiration from the oldest geometric forms in human civilization.
It brings together precise mathematical principles and the purity of artistic form, using holographic projection to move beyond the solid limits of traditional sculpture. Through flowing light, slender visual structures, and a floating presentation, it expresses the ease with which technological reason shapes spatial order.
Its stable, restrained composition gives physical balance an almost ideal, unshakable presence.
The artist placed the installation in the square before the Olympia Art Gallery, echoing the early Golden Age museum philosophy of creating a dialogue between history and the present.
In doing so, the work forms a layered narrative across space and time, extending its aesthetic meaning into the construction of the surrounding environment.
Whether you're looking toward the future or back to the past, it serves as a guiding beacon.

Title: A Glance Back: Defining Moments in Human History
Content:
Looking back at the decisive moments of history, we revisit the turning points of human civilization.
This exhibition brings together treasured paintings, sculptures, and installations from artists of different schools, weaving a complete thread of humanity's shared destiny.
Since the signing of The New Earth Codex, humanity has formally declared itself a single civilization bound by shared fate.
In the Golden Age ushered in by the activation of the Gestalt system, we created and shared a brilliance never seen before.
When the zero-point reactor accident triggered an apocalyptic disaster, we became one another's vessel, crossing the chasm of civilizational rupture together.
The era of the Great Evacuation was lit by sacrifice and hope, preserving the spark of human civilization, until the horn of counterattack sounded and proclaimed our unyielding will to the universe.
The weight of these "moments" becomes signposts guiding the future.
Each time we look back at history, it is so we may face what lies ahead with greater resolve.

Title: Negative Memories Shape Reality: A Spatial Reconstruction of Collective Memory
Content:
This exhibition explores the latest practice of "Negative Formism" through its integration with social psychology, bringing living historical memory into solid architectural space.
The artists gathered testimonies from those who lived through the Great Evacuation, transforming collective memory into three-dimensional, dynamic sketch imagery that gives memory physical presence in the real world.
At key moments of collective trauma, the artists intentionally leave areas empty through the use of negative space. Emotional responses captured from witnesses through neural staining are translated by algorithms into color, then projected across these blank sections of the exhibition floor.
Through this contrast between absence and presence, Negative Formism reflects on the loss of individual emotion under technological rationality, using what is missing to reveal the wounds of an era.

Title: The Shape of Growth: The Metabolism of Artistic Life
Content:
This exhibition presents nine new works from the emerging art movement known as "Metabolism," shown together to the public for the first time.
The artists integrate biological metabolic processes into their creations, cultivating new biomaterials and allowing the works to take shape through natural growth and change.
During the exhibition, visitors can take part in this evolving process within cultivation frameworks designed by the artists, influencing factors such as temperature, humidity, and light.
The result is a temporary art experience co-created by artists and viewers alike. Each work exists in a state of irreversible transformation and fading, inviting reflection on the nature of life, time, and existence.

Title: Revival Silverthread
Content: Appearance: The plant forms an exquisite cluster with leaves as fine as silver threads, typically glowing with a cool silver-green metallic sheen. When the eco-chamber simulates extreme drought, it curls into a gray-brown ball, seemingly lifeless. However, once simulated "moisture" nutrients are introduced, the leaves quickly unfurl within seconds, returning to their dynamic silver-threaded state as if they had never withered.\nType: Fern. A genetically optimized "recovery-type" conservation plant.\nSignificance: A star species of Babylonia's eco-laboratory. The original variety nearly went extinct due to Earth's Red Tide phenomenon. Through precise eco-chamber cultivation, its numbers are steadily recovering. The "dehydration dormancy—water-triggered recovery" mechanism encoded in its genes has been a focal point for scientific study. These optimized plants are set to become "ecological vanguards" in Earth's deserts and harsh dry regions, proving through cycles of withering and revival that life can endure even in extreme conditions. They offer hope for rebuilding green spaces in barren lands.

Title: Dome Tortoiseshell Banana
Content: Appearance: Broad, plantain-like leaves in deep green, patterned with regular perforations reminiscent of turtle shells with a futuristic edge. The plant stands tall, crowned with cream-colored spathe blooms. Under simulated eco-chamber lighting, the leaf patterns refract a faint blue glow.\nType: Angiosperm. A genetically optimized high-oxygen tropical plant.\nSignificance: One of the core species in the Oxygen Factory program. After a severe decline due to atmospheric pollution and habitat loss on Earth, eco-chamber cultivation greatly enhanced its photosynthetic efficiency. It converts carbon dioxide into oxygen at high rates, while its perforated leaves and genetic resilience allow adaptation to harsh environments. These plants are expected to play a key role in restoring tropical surface ecosystems and offer valuable reference data for life-support systems, earning them the name oxygen messengers beneath the green dome.

Title: Vibrant Dome Aroid
Content: Appearance: A tall, upright plant with heart-shaped leaves. The primary plant bears deep green foliage with clearly defined veins and a subtle metallic sheen. The mutated plant displays vivid leaves that shift from purple-black to bright orange-red, resembling burning neon flames under eco-chamber lighting.\nType: Angiosperm. A large ornamental foliage plant with genetically optimized color mutation.\nSignificance: A representative species of genetic diversity. The original plant declined sharply due to ecological damage and overharvesting on Earth. Through precise eco-chamber cultivation, its resilience was preserved while rare color mutations were induced. The environmental adaptation and phenotypic variation encoded in its genes provide valuable samples for studying plant evolution under extreme conditions. With further genetic optimization, it may one day grow in heavily polluted surface regions, using its vivid foliage as a natural ecological indicator.

Title: Twins Dome Aroid
Content: Appearance: A twin-growth plant. The primary plant bears broad, heart-shaped jade-green leaves with clearly defined silver-gray veins and a rich, glossy texture. The secondary plant displays leaves that shift from deep purple to dark crimson, as if touched by interstellar afterglow, creating a striking contrast under eco-chamber lighting.\nType: Angiosperm. A large ornamental foliage plant with a genetically edited symbiotic mutation.\nSignificance: The original species neared extinction after Earth's ecosystem collapsed. Cultivation within Babylonia's eco-chambers produced a rare twin mutation, demonstrating the possibility of symbiotic evolution under artificial conditions. Its genetic samples offer key insight into resource allocation and phenotypic change in extreme environments. In the future, it may serve as a pioneer symbiote for restoring fragmented surface ecosystems, while standing as a living example of genetic diversity conservation and life's ability to adapt under pressure.

Title: Just a Pothos
Content: Appearance: Heart-shaped leaves with a deep green base color and faint blue-violet halos between the veins (a subtle mutation caused by long-term exposure to Babylonia's eco-chamber environment). The vines are flexible and abundant, naturally cascading or clinging to eco-chamber mechanical structures, creating a "green waterfall." The leaf halos shift slightly with changes in environmental humidity, responding to light.\nType: Angiosperm. An Araceae family "general-purpose" ornamental plant that has developed phenotypic mutations due to long-term adaptation to artificial environments.\nSignificance: The most "ordinary" yet warmest presence in the ecological garden. Originally a common pothos casually transplanted by an early Babylonia logistics worker from Earth's ruins, it was planted in the eco-chamber's corner because it was easy to maintain. Unexpectedly, it took root and thrived in this artificial environment, with generations of staff caring for it, forming this lush ecosystem. It lacks the rarity of endangered species but holds unique "heritage significance"—witnessing the growth of Babylonia and carrying the staff's simple affection for Earth's native plants. Under the steel dome, it stands as a living green imprint born from a simple act of "casual planting."

Title: Babylonia Edible Products Ecological Research Report (Briefing)
Content:
Reporter: Zhi Ben
This study systematically explores a growing contradiction in Babylonia's dietary ecosystem: While nutritional science reveals the profound benefits of food diversity for human health, the structural homogeneity of Babylonia's vegetable supply system poses a potential public health risk. Dietary diversity, particularly the variety of vegetables and fruits, plays a crucial role in regulating gut microbiota and is closely linked to a reduction in depression risk. This connection is tied to people's mental state, one aspect of which includes various forms of homesickness.
The current issues in Babylonia's dietary ecosystem are as follows:
1. Delayed wartime production planning and high reliance on synthetic nutrition products:
Since the Red Tide crisis, large cultivation fields have been used to grow high-yield crops like potatoes, cassava, and sweet potatoes to address food supply and war preparedness. This led to a significant shortage of vegetables and fruits in the short term. Attempts have been made to fill this gap, but the logic of production recovery followed market demand rather than ecological health principles. Crops with high market demand, like lettuce and apples, were prioritized.
During this period, Babylonia's nutritional balance relied heavily on synthetic food products. Compared to fresh vegetables, these products offer poorer texture and a monotonous taste. As construction enters a recovery phase and overall conditions gradually improve, synthetic nutrition alone can no longer meet people's recovering psychological and emotional needs. Addressing flavor, enjoyment, and the human experience of eating should therefore become a priority.
2. A major gap in dietary variety:
This gap appears in two key areas.
First, a lack of cultural diversity. Wartime food control prioritizes efficiency, often at the expense of cultural variety. When people go long periods without the flavors of home, stress builds up and may lead to mild depressive symptoms.
Second, a lack of climatic diversity. Babylonia's production lines mainly simulate temperate and subtropical climates, leaving little room for tropical or cold-region crops. Prolonged life in a space-station greenhouse can create a sense of disconnection from past experiences. The Science Council refers to this condition as "Space Station Perceptual Alienation Syndrome." Increasing climatic diversity in food production may help alleviate this effect.
3. Additional objective production constraints:
Limited cultivation space and crop growth cycles are objective factors restricting agricultural diversity in Babylonia. The fragility of surface conservation areas also makes access to diverse food sources unstable. The report recommends relocating selected production lines to the surface when conditions allow and improving ground-to-space transport routes. These measures should be key priorities in future reconstruction and long-term ecological planning.
